Foundations of mathematics

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 199k Articles: 4k
Foundations of mathematics asks what our objects mean, what we assume about them, and why an argument establishes its conclusion. Set theory gives a common language for collections and functions; mathematical logic makes the structure of statements and deductions precise. A mathematical definition fixes a meaning, an axiom supplies an assumption, and a mathematical proof explains what follows. Separating these roles makes results reusable: once the group axioms are enough for a conclusion, that conclusion applies to every group, regardless of how its members are represented.
The assumptions can change the answer to a familiar calculation. Over the real numbers, x2=x factors as x(x−1)=0, so x is zero or one. The same reasoning holds in any integral domain, because a product can be zero only when a factor is zero. In the ring of integers modulo six, however, 32≡3 and 42≡4(mod6): there are four solutions, represented by 0,1,3,4. The extra solutions are idempotents, and the failed step involves zero divisors. Writing the domain is part of explaining the answer.
This precision also reveals surprising possibilities. A two-dimensional grid of natural numbers is a countable set, while all infinite binary sequences form an uncountable set. The Cantor pairing function supplies a complete enumeration of the first; Cantor's diagonal argument defeats every proposed enumeration of the second. Both arguments are short, yet distinguish two sizes of infinity. The subject's appeal is this ability to turn a vague question into one whose assumptions, construction, and limits can all be inspected.

Mathematical definition

Words: 54
Foundations of mathematics OurBigBook.com
A specification of the meaning of a mathematical term or notation. A structural definition specifies conditions, such as the group axioms; a definition by a universal property characterizes an object by its arrows. Such a characterization does not by itself prove that the object exists. For example, existence of an exponential object is an additional property of a category.

Pushdown automaton

Words: 128 Articles: 2
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A finite control equipped with an unbounded stack. A move reads one input symbol or the empty word, examines the top stack symbol, changes control state and replaces that top by a finite word over the stack alphabet. Nondeterministic choices give finitely many possible moves. With acceptance by final state and the entire input consumed, pushdown automata recognize exactly the context-free languages.

Acceptance by final state

Words: 34
Pushdown automaton OurBigBook.com
A pushdown automaton accepts a word if some finite run consumes all its input and reaches a designated final control state, regardless of the remaining stack contents. Reaching a final control state while leaving unread input is insufficient.

Pushdown automaton configuration ((q,w,α))

Words: 43
Pushdown automaton OurBigBook.com
The control state q, unread input word w, and stack contents α of a pushdown automaton. A fixed convention must say which end of α is the top. With the top on the left, replacing top X by γ changes Xβ into γβ.

Finite language

Words: 26
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A formal language with finitely many words. Every finite language is a regular language: take a finite union of the regular expressions spelling its members, with the empty language represented separately when there are no members.

Shuffle of formal languages (L1​⊕L2​)

Words: 46
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
The shuffle of two formal languages consists of words whose positions can be partitioned into two subsequences, each preserving its order, with the two resulting words belonging to the respective languages. For regular languages, a product-state nondeterministic finite automaton advances exactly one coordinate for each letter. Common letters allow either choice; the powerset construction proves closure.

Left quotient of a formal language (u−1L)

Words: 43
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
For a word u and a formal language L, the left quotient u−1L={w:uw∈L} is the possible continuation language after the prefix u. Two prefixes have the same left quotient exactly when they are Myhill-Nerode equivalent. For a regular language only finitely many distinct left quotients occur.

Padded convolution of words (u⊗v)

Words: 48
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
The padded convolution of words reads two finite words over an alphabet in parallel, extending the shorter with a fresh padding symbol # until the longer ends. Its length is max(∣u∣,∣v∣). Padding may only occur as a suffix, and a (#,#) column is excluded. This encodes synchronous two-tape relations as formal languages over a finite paired alphabet.

Recursive language

Words: 104 Articles: 1
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A formal language is decidable if a Turing machine halts on every input and correctly determines membership. Equivalently its encoded words form a recursive set. A computably enumerable language requires only a machine that eventually accepts every member; it may run forever on nonmembers.

Threshold language (La​={enc(n):n≥a})

Words: 68
Recursive language OurBigBook.com
For a fixed natural number a and a standard encoding of natural numbers, validate the input and compare its encoded value with a. This decides La​. A well-ordering argument can prove that an upward-closed set of natural numbers has this form without calculating its least element. A decider may contain that fixed least element in its finite description; its existence does not give a uniform method to discover the least element from another program.

String

Words: 462 Articles: 15
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A word over an alphabet Σ is a finite sequence of symbols from Σ. The empty word has length zero, and Σ∗ denotes the set of all finite words.

Case-insensitive comparison

Words: 34
String OurBigBook.com
A comparison of strings that disregards a chosen distinction between uppercase and lowercase characters. A simple convention compares characterwise lowercase forms. Full Unicode case folding is a distinct normalization operation and can change character counts.

Longest common prefix (LCP(s,t))

Words: 65
String OurBigBook.com
The longest common prefix of two strings is the longest string that is a string prefix of both. Its length is the number of matching initial characters before the first mismatch or the end of a string. A direct scan maintains equality of the processed prefixes and takes time linear in that length plus one. For suffixes represented by indices in a shared array, no character copying is needed.

String suffix

Words: 40
String OurBigBook.com
A string suffix consists of all characters from some position to the end of a string. For example, TAC has suffixes TAC, AC, C and the empty string. Sorting these in lexicographic order groups all suffixes beginning with a given query into one interval.

Cyclic rotation

Words: 38
String OurBigBook.com
A cyclic rotation of a string xy is the string yx, where x and y are consecutive pieces. For example, rotating ABC left once gives BCA. A length-n string has n rotation positions, though repeated letters can make some resulting strings identical.

String rewriting

String OurBigBook.com

Substring

Words: 21
String OurBigBook.com
A substring is a contiguous segment of a string. It differs from a subsequence, whose selected characters need not be adjacent.

Sturmian word

Words: 22 Articles: 1
String OurBigBook.com
An infinite binary word is Sturmian if it has exactly n+1 distinct contiguous subwords of length n for every positive integer n.
Characteristic Sturmian word
Sturmian word OurBigBook.com

Palindrome

Words: 50 Articles: 1
String OurBigBook.com
A palindrome is a finite string equal to its reversal. For example, the strings 010 and 0110 are palindromes.
Palindrome test
Words: 32
Palindrome OurBigBook.com
Decide whether a finite string is a palindrome by comparing corresponding symbols from opposite ends. The test needs at most half as many symbol comparisons as the string length and can use constant auxiliary space.

Anagram

String OurBigBook.com

Concatenation (uv)

Words: 43
String OurBigBook.com
Concatenation joins two strings end to end, retaining the order of their symbols. For example, joining ab and ba gives abba. It has the associative property: joining (uv)w or u(vw) gives the same word over an alphabet. The empty word is its identity element. All finite words over an alphabet with this binary operation form a free monoid.

Length of a word over an alphabet (ℓ(w))

Words: 38
String OurBigBook.com
The length of a word over an alphabet is the number of symbol positions in that finite string, counting repetitions. Thus ℓ(abba)=4 and ℓ(ε)=0 for the empty word. Concatenation satisfies ℓ(uv)=ℓ(u)+ℓ(v). This differs from the word length of a group element, which minimizes over representing words using a chosen generating set of a group.

Run of a word

Words: 45
String OurBigBook.com
A run of a word over an alphabet is a maximal consecutive block of one repeated letter. For a nonempty word w of length N, its number of runs is
R(w)=1+∑j=1N−1​1{wj​=wj+1​}​.
(1)
Replacing a consecutive constant block changes this count only through its boundaries with the neighboring letters.

Border of a word

Words: 36
String OurBigBook.com
A border of a word is a nonempty prefix that is also a suffix. The full word is counted as a border; a shorter border records a way in which one occurrence can overlap the next.

Regular expression

Words: 75 Articles: 2
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A regular expression is built from alphabet symbols, the empty language and the empty word using finite union, concatenation and Kleene star.

Kleene star (L∗)

Words: 22
Regular expression OurBigBook.com
The Kleene star L∗ of a language L consists of every finite concatenation of words from L, including the empty concatenation.

Kleene theorem

Words: 31
Regular expression OurBigBook.com
This theorem characterizes a regular language by regular expressions and acceptance by a finite-state automaton. Kleene's theorem states that a language is denoted by a regular expression exactly when it is accepted by a finite automaton.

Formal grammar

Words: 402 Articles: 14
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A grammar (N,Σ,P,S) generates the terminal words reachable from S by finitely many productions.

Formation rule

Words: 23
Formal grammar OurBigBook.com
A formation rule specifies how well-formed expressions can be constructed from simpler expressions in a formal language. The formal grammar of propositional formulas has rules for propositional variables, negation and binary logical implication.

Variable-based grammar

Words: 365 Articles: 12
Formal grammar OurBigBook.com
A variable-based grammar has disjoint finite terminal and variable alphabets Σ,V, a start variable S∈V, and productions α→β in which α,β∈(Σ∪V)∗ and α contains at least one variable.
Unreachable nonterminal
Words: 27
Variable-based grammar OurBigBook.com
A nonterminal is unreachable when no word derivable from the start symbol contains it. Productions whose left sides are unreachable do not affect the generated language.
Nonproductive nonterminal
Words: 32
Variable-based grammar OurBigBook.com
A nonterminal is nonproductive when no word derived from it consists entirely of terminal symbols. Every derivation containing such a symbol therefore fails to produce a word in the generated language.
Regular grammar
Words: 127 Articles: 5
Variable-based grammar OurBigBook.com
A right-linear regular grammar has productions of the forms A→wB and A→w, where A,B are variables and w is a terminal word.
Sentential form of a right-linear regular grammar
Words: 33
Regular grammar OurBigBook.com
Every sentential form reachable from the start variable of a right-linear grammar is either a terminal word w or wA, where A is the unique variable and occurs at the right end.
Accessible variable of a regular grammar
Words: 13
Regular grammar OurBigBook.com
A variable A is accessible when S⇒∗wA for some terminal word w.
Looping variable of a regular grammar
Words: 16
Regular grammar OurBigBook.com
A variable A is looping when A⇒∗wA for some terminal word w through a nonempty derivation.
Terminable variable of a regular grammar
Words: 13
Regular grammar OurBigBook.com
A variable A is terminable when A⇒∗w for some terminal word w.
Accessible looping terminable variable criterion
Words: 27
Regular grammar OurBigBook.com
If a finite right-linear grammar generates an infinite language, some variable is accessible, looping, and terminable. It is the repeated variable on a sufficiently long accepting derivation.
Concatenation grammar
Words: 147 Articles: 3
Variable-based grammar OurBigBook.com
For grammars G=(Σ,V,P,S) and G′=(Σ,V′,P′,S′) with disjoint variable sets, introduce a new variable S0​ and set
H=(Σ,V∪V′∪{S0​},P∪P′∪{S0​→SS′},S0​).
(2)
If both input grammars are variable based, then L(H)=L(G)L(G′).
Regular concatenation grammar
Words: 89 Articles: 1
Concatenation grammar OurBigBook.com
Retain every production α→β of P whose right-hand side contains a variable, replace every production α→w with w∈Σ∗ by α→wS′, include P′, and use S as start variable. If G and G′ are right-linear, the resulting grammar is right-linear and generates L(G)L(G′).
Failure of the regular concatenation construction for a nonregular grammar
Words: 42
Regular concatenation grammar OurBigBook.com
The regular construction relies on a regular derivation having exactly one terminal rule, at its end. In a general variable-based grammar several variables may each use terminal productions, so replacing every such production can introduce several copies of the second start variable.
Concatenation grammar need not be regular
Words: 27
Concatenation grammar OurBigBook.com
Even if both input grammars are regular, the added production S0​→SS′ has two variables on its right-hand side and therefore need not be a regular production.

Empty word (ϵ)

Words: 17
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
The empty word is the unique word of length zero. It is the identity element for concatenation.

Context-free language

Words: 991 Articles: 28
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A grammar is context-free when each production has one nonterminal on its left.

Suffix-nonnegative binary language ({w: ∣v∣0​≥∣v∣1​ for every suffix v of w})

Words: 79
Context-free language OurBigBook.com
A context-free language recognized by scanning a string over the alphabet {0,1} from right to left, counting 0 as +1 and 1 as −1, and requiring every partial count to remain nonnegative. A context-free grammar with a unique parse tree for each generated string is S→ϵ∣S0∣S1B0, B→ϵ∣B1B0. To see uniqueness, reverse the strings: every nonempty nonnegative path either never returns to zero after its first step, or has a unique first return. These two cases determine the production and its component substrings.

Context-free grammar

Words: 730 Articles: 19
Context-free language OurBigBook.com
A context-free grammar consists of terminal and nonterminal alphabets, a start symbol, and productions whose left side is one nonterminal. A derivation records the order of substitutions, while a parse tree records their hierarchical structure, so several derivations can represent one parse tree.
Conversion of a context-free grammar to a pushdown automaton
Words: 66
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
Store the start nonterminal symbol on a stack. An epsilon transition nondeterministically replaces its top nonterminal symbol by a production rule right-hand side. A top terminal symbol can be removed only while consuming the same input symbol. With a protected stack bottom marker, enter a final control state when that marker is exposed. Requiring all input to have been read implements acceptance by final state. The stack records the unprocessed suffix of a leftmost derivation, proving equality of the recognized and generated formal languages.
Ambiguous grammar
Words: 33
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
A context-free grammar is ambiguous when some accepted token sequence has two distinct parse trees. Giving a language an unambiguous context-free grammar requires specifying grouping in the productions themselves, rather than relying on an unstated parser conflict rule.
Semantic action
Words: 24
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
An operation associated with a context-free grammar production, performed when that production is recognized. Semantic actions can construct an abstract syntax tree by combining the trees attached to its child nonterminal symbols.
Right-linear grammar
Words: 73
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
A right-linear grammar has productions of the form A→wB or A→w, where A,B are nonterminals and w is a terminal word, possibly empty. Each right-hand side has at most one nonterminal, at its right end. Such grammars generate exactly regular languages: regard nonterminals as states and expand each terminal word into a finite path to another state or an accepting endpoint. Conversely the transition graph of a deterministic finite automaton gives these productions directly.
Terminal symbol
Words: 18
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
A terminal symbol belongs to the alphabet of completed words and is not replaced by a grammar production.
Production rule
Words: 25
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
A production rule specifies a permitted replacement during a grammar derivation. In a context-free grammar it has the form A→α, with one nonterminal A on the left.
Sentence of a formal grammar
Words: 14
Context-free grammar OurBigBook.com
A sentence of a grammar is a terminal word derivable from its start symbol.

A grammar derivation is a finite sequence of words in which each step replaces one occurrence of a production's left side by its right side. A leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost available nonterminal.
Leftmost derivation

Grammar derivation OurBigBook.com
A grammar derivation that always expands the leftmost remaining nonterminal symbol. In a context-free grammar, each parse tree specifies exactly one leftmost derivation. Two distinct leftmost derivations of the same word therefore prove that the context-free grammar is an ambiguous grammar.

A parse tree places the start symbol at its root, the symbols on the right side of a production at the children of its left-side nonterminal, and terminal symbols at its leaves. Reading the leaves from left to right gives the tree's yield.

Conversion of a context-free grammar to Chomsky normal form
Words: 77
Chomsky normal form OurBigBook.com
To convert a context-free grammar to Chomsky normal form, first add a fresh start symbol. Remove epsilon productions, retaining the exceptional start production only when the empty word is to remain in the language; then remove unit productions and symbols that cannot participate in a terminal derivation. Replace each terminal occurring in a right-hand side of length at least two by a new nonterminal that produces that terminal. Finally split every right-hand side of length greater than two into binary productions using fresh nonterminals.
Chomsky-normal-form derivation length
Words: 29
Chomsky normal form OurBigBook.com
A Chomsky-normal-form parse tree for a word of length n≥1 has n terminal productions and n−1 binary productions. Every derivation represented by the tree therefore has exactly 2n−1 steps.
CYK algorithm
Words: 46
Chomsky normal form OurBigBook.com
The CYK algorithm decides membership in a context-free language given by a grammar in Chomsky normal form. It records, for every substring, the nonterminals that derive that substring and combines adjacent substrings using binary productions. For a word of length n and a fixed grammar, it runs in O(n3) time.

Weak Chomsky normal form additionally permits ternary productions A→BCD. Compressing a two-step pattern A→BE, E→CD into A→BCD preserves its generated yields whenever the intermediate variable has no other role, and saves one derivation step each time the pattern is used.

Finite-state machine

Words: 3k Articles: 54
Formal language theory OurBigBook.com
A finite-state machine processes inputs using a finite set of automaton states and input-dependent automaton transitions. An automaton state records everything the machine remembers; an automaton transition says how that memory changes on the next symbol. A finite-state machine may also emit outputs. Here the emphasis is on recognizing a formal language: start in a designated automaton state, read a word from an alphabet, and accept exactly when the final automaton state is designated accepting.
Finite memory does not impose a maximum input length. A finite-state machine can read arbitrarily long words, revisiting its automaton states indefinitely. The restriction is that the part already read must be compressed into one of finitely many summaries. For divisibility by three, a word of binary digits can describe an enormous integer, yet its congruence class modulo three is all that the machine needs to retain. Two already-read words giving the same automaton state behave identically under every subsequent continuation in a DFA.
This makes finite-state machines useful whenever past details can be forgotten safely: checking whether a sequence of commands follows an allowed order, or recognizing a pattern with a regular expression. The beautiful design question is which distinctions about the past matter to the future. DFA minimization makes that question precise by merging indistinguishable states of a deterministic finite automaton. Both DFAs and NFAs recognize exactly the regular languages.

Self-starting finite-state machine

Finite-state machine OurBigBook.com
A hardware finite-state machine whose implemented transitions eventually leave every unused state encoding and enter the intended valid state set. If recovery must hold for arbitrary inputs, it is not enough that some input sequence can escape: there must be no indefinitely surviving unused-state path under any input sequence. A reset or initialization rule may still be required to give the valid state its intended meaning.

Interrupt-driven pulse sequencer

Finite-state machine OurBigBook.com
A pulse sequencer can separate event capture from output timing. A short interrupt handler acknowledges the event latch and increments a pending count. An independent finite-state machine consumes one count on entering ON, changes to GAP after the pulse width, and enters IDLE only after the mandatory off interval. Even an empty queue must not bypass GAP: an arrival immediately after light-off would otherwise start too soon.
The pending count equals recorded events minus started pulses. A critical section protects its read-modify-write operations; declaring shared state as in volatile-qualified objects in C does not alone make each update an atomic operation. Separate sequencers for different channels allow simultaneous pulses while one hardware timer schedules their earliest deadline. Finite queue capacity, detector rearming and dispatch resolution remain explicit assumptions.

Prefix-suffix sequence recognizer
Words: 134
Moore machine OurBigBook.com
For a fixed word w, store the length of the longest suffix of the received stream that is also a prefix of w. On a new input symbol, append it to the represented prefix and select the longest resulting suffix that is a prefix of w. The complete-word state signals recognition. Its outgoing transitions retain proper suffix matches, allowing overlapping occurrences rather than automatically restarting from the empty prefix. This is the finite-state form of the prefix information used by the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm.
For example, recognizing 1101 needs suffix-prefix states of lengths zero through four. After a complete match followed by one, the last two symbols are 11, so the next state retains length two. This permits the second match in 1101101 without clearing the useful suffix.

c=a∧p∧q,d=¬a∧¬p∧¬q,(p′,q′)=(a,p),e′=d∨(e∧¬c),z′=z⊕(e∧c).
(5)
The two three-sample run detectors cannot assert simultaneously. A high run toggles once and clears e; only a complete low run rearms it. All right-hand sides use the old state, so the toggling event occurs at the third qualifying clock edge.
The controller has twelve distinguishable behaviours: for each z, three armed states count trailing highs of lengths 0,1,2, and three disarmed states count trailing lows of lengths 0,1,2. The run lengths are distinguished by the number of further matching samples needed before a toggle or rearm. Armed and disarmed states are distinguished by an all-high continuation. Thus at least ⌈log2​12⌉=4 state bits are required, and the displayed design attains that bound.

Deterministic finite automaton

Words: 810 Articles: 14
Finite-state machine OurBigBook.com
A deterministic finite automaton has exactly one automaton transition for every automaton state and input symbol. Formally, a DFA is a tuple (Q,Σ,δ,q0​,F): Q is a nonempty finite set of automaton states, Σ a finite alphabet, δ:Q×Σ→Q a function, q0​ the initial automaton state, and F⊆Q the accepting automaton states. Its unique path on a word accepts if it ends in F after consuming the entire input. Visiting F earlier does not suffice.
For a concrete binary divisibility automaton, recognize the words whose values in the binary numeral system are divisible by three. Choose Q={0,1,2}, Σ={0,1}, q0​=0, and F={0}. Each automaton state names the congruence class of the integer read so far. Appending a binary digit b changes its value n to 2n+b, so the automaton transition is
δ(r,b)=(2r+b)mod3.
(6)
The modular arithmetic therefore needs only three automaton states, whatever the input length. The full function is δ(0,0)=0, δ(0,1)=1, δ(1,0)=2, δ(1,1)=0, δ(2,0)=1, and δ(2,1)=2.
For 1102​=6, the successive automaton states are 0→1→0→0, so the word is accepted. For 1012​=5, they are 0→1→2→2, so it is rejected. Leading zeros are allowed: they leave the initial automaton state unchanged. We explicitly assign value zero to the empty word, which is accepted because the initial automaton state is accepting. This is a convention for a formal language, rather than a claim that ordinary written numerals include a blank numeral.
The generator checks every word of up to eight binary digits, comparing the final automaton state with the integer value modulo three. Each length n includes all 2n words, preserving leading zeros as distinct inputs:

All 511 checks agree. They are useful for catching a reversed arrow or mistaken label, but the reason the DFA works at every length is its invariant: after reading any word of value n, its automaton state is nmod3. The update n↦2n+b preserves that statement by mathematical induction. Through the extended transition function of a deterministic finite automaton, this becomes δ(0,w)=value(w)mod3.

Nondeterministic finite automaton

Words: 629 Articles: 9
Finite-state machine OurBigBook.com
A nondeterministic finite automaton allows a set of possible destinations for each automaton state and input symbol. Without the extra moves permitted in an Epsilon-NFA, replace the DFA function by Δ:Q×Σ→P(Q), where P(Q) is the power set. A word is accepted when at least one path consumes all its symbols and ends in an accepting automaton state. These choices express existential quantification, not probability: no chance of choosing a particular path is assigned. One successful path suffices even if other paths fail.
Consider a three-state NFA accepting exactly the words of binary digits ending in 01. Its initial automaton state q0​ loops on both 0 and 1; it also has an automaton transition q0​0​q1​, followed by q1​1​q2​. Only q2​ is accepting, and all unlisted automaton transitions are absent. Staying at q0​ skips an arbitrary beginning; leaving it guesses that the current zero starts the final two symbols.
The word 01 accepts along q0​→q1​→q2​. The word 1101 accepts along q0​→q0​→q0​→q1​→q2​. The word 010 rejects: a path reaching q2​ after 01 cannot consume the remaining zero, while the other paths end outside q2​. Thus finding 01 somewhere is insufficient; it must occur at the end.
To simulate the NFA deterministically, retain the set S of all currently possible automaton states. The powerset construction updates S by taking the union of the destinations of its members. Here only {q0​}, {q0​,q1​}, and {q0​,q2​} are reachable, although the full power set has eight members. Reading 010 gives {q0​}→{q0​,q1​}→{q0​,q2​}→{q0​,q1​}, which rejects. In general, an N-state NFA yields a DFA with at most 2N automaton states. Nondeterminism can simplify a description, while the powerset construction keeps the memory finite.
The second generator checks all 511 words of up to eight binary digits against the direct test of whether their final two symbols are 01. Exactly 127 accept, and only the three listed sets of automaton states occur. In particular, the empty word rejects for this NFA.
Michael O. Rabin and Dana Scott's 1959 paper studied finite-state machines as recognizers with finite internal memory. Every accepting run makes exactly one of the additional moves.

For a sample term max{0,1−ai​x}, the active hinge set contains indices with 1−ai​x>0. Stability (learning theory)

Words: 62 Articles: 1
Statistical learning theory OurBigBook.com
In statistical learning theory, Stability measures how much a learned predictor or its loss changes when the training sample is perturbed. Uniform stability of a learning algorithm imposes a bound valid at every test example.

Uniform stability of a learning algorithm

Words: 36
Stability (learning theory) OurBigBook.com
This is a uniform version of Stability for learning algorithms. A learning algorithm has uniform stability β for a loss when replacing one training example changes the loss at every test example by at most β.

Decision tree learning

Words: 225 Articles: 4
Statistical learning theory OurBigBook.com
Decision tree learning fits predictors by recursively partitioning input space. Leaves predict labels for classification or numerical values for regression; a regression tree is the numerical-response case.

Regression tree

Words: 203 Articles: 3
Decision tree learning OurBigBook.com
A regression tree is the numerical-response case of decision tree learning. A regression tree recursively partitions predictor space by axis-aligned splits. At each leaf, candidate coordinates and thresholds are compared by the residual sum of squares after replacing that leaf by its two children; the selected split minimizes the total criterion. The fitted value in each terminal region is the sample mean there.
Decision stump
Words: 105 Articles: 1
Regression tree OurBigBook.com
A decision stump is a decision tree with one split. A regression stump predicts a constant, usually the sample mean, in each of its two terminal regions.
Weighted decision stump optimization
Words: 80
Decision stump OurBigBook.com
For stumps h(x)=sign(xi​−b) of fixed polarity, sort observations along each coordinate and sweep the threshold across whole groups of equal values. Passing a group adds its positive-label weight and subtracts its negative-label weight from the weighted misclassification risk. Include thresholds below and above all observed values. Every distinct sample prediction pattern is considered, giving exact minimization in O(nmlogm) time complexity for m observations in Rn. Coordinate sort orders can be reused across AdaBoost rounds, reducing subsequent weighted scans to O(nm).

Mathematical proof

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Foundations of mathematics OurBigBook.com
A mathematical proof is a finite deductive argument from stated assumptions to a conclusion. It explains why the conclusion follows for every instance covered by its hypotheses. An informal mathematical proof can omit routine detail while making its assumptions and deductions clear; a formal proof expresses them in a specified formal language with specified inference rules. The distinction between assumptions, propositions, and deductions is introduced in Leighton and Rubinfeld, What is a proof?, sections 1–3.
Checking examples can suggest a pattern, but need not establish a universally quantified claim. For example, the polynomial n2+n+41 is a prime number for every integer 0≤n≤39, as direct trial division verifies. At n=40 it equals 1681=412, a composite number. Those first forty successes do not prove the claim for all natural numbers; one counterexample disproves it. The point is not to discard computation: it can find a conjecture, detect a mistake, or verify a finite exhaustive case analysis. The question is whether the cases checked cover the statement being claimed.
For a positive example, the sum of two even integers is even: writing them as 2a and 2b with a,b∈Z gives 2a+2b=2(a+b), and a+b is an integer. This direct argument handles every allowed pair at once. A useful mathematical proof therefore does more than certify an answer: it exposes the mechanism and the exact assumptions that make the answer transferable.

Equational reasoning

Words: 51
Mathematical proof OurBigBook.com
Prove equality of expressions through a chain of substitutions justified by definitions, previously established equalities, or algebraic laws. Each step preserves the expression's value. In a programming language with lazy evaluation, an asserted program law must also preserve termination and the demanded amount of a partial value, not just agree on finite defined inputs.

Reductio ad absurdum ((¬P⇒⊥)⇒P)

Words: 60
Mathematical proof OurBigBook.com
A reductio rejects an assumption by deriving an absurd or contradictory consequence from it. In a classical mathematical proof of P, assume its negation and derive a contradiction. Constructively the same argument yields the double negation of P; removing it requires an additional logical principle. This differs from proving a negation directly by deriving a contradiction from the positive assumption.

Mathematical induction (P(n0​),P(n)⇒P(n+1))

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Mathematical proof OurBigBook.com
A mathematical induction proof establishes a property P(n) for every integer n≥n0​ by proving its induction base case and its inductive step. If a counterexample existed, the well-ordering principle would give a least one; its predecessor and the inductive implication exclude it. The starting case excludes a counterexample at n0​.
The useful idea is to cover infinitely many cases with two finite pieces of reasoning. The induction base case starts the chain, and the inductive step shows that success at an arbitrary stage propagates to the next. It is especially natural when a construction adds one item at a time: another row of a diagram, another input processed by an algorithm, or another term of a sequence. The loop invariant method is the same propagation idea applied to successive stages of a computation.
For the triangular number Tn​=1+2+⋯+n, the proposed formula is Tn​=n(n+1)/2. At n=1, both sides are one. Assuming the formula for a fixed positive integer n, add the next row:
Tn+1​=Tn​+(n+1)=2n(n+1)​+(n+1)=2(n+1)(n+2)​.
(41)
This is the desired formula at n+1, proving the inductive step. For example, T5​=15 and T6​=15+6=21; these numerical cases illustrate the general step rather than replace it.
The second picture explains where the formula comes from: two copies of the triangular arrangement tile an n by n+1 rectangle. Thus 2Tn​=n(n+1). The mathematical induction argument certifies how the formula continues, while the rearrangement makes its factors visible. Neither picture is restricted to the five rows drawn: both constructions are specified for every positive integer n.

Recursion theorem on the natural numbers (f(0)=a,f(n+1)=H(n,f(n)))

Words: 52
Mathematical induction OurBigBook.com
Given an initial value a and a specified successor rule on a set, there is a unique function on the natural numbers with that initial value and successor rule. Finite compatible approximations give existence; induction gives agreement of any two approximations and uniqueness. Recursive definitions of addition and multiplication apply this theorem with the other argument fixed.

Inductive step (P(n)⇒P(n+1))

Words: 40
Mathematical induction OurBigBook.com
Assuming the induction hypothesis for a fixed integer, establish the next instance. Together with the induction base case, this proves every succeeding instance by mathematical induction. The hypothesis is conditional within this argument, rather than an unsupported assumption that the desired theorem is already true.

Induction base case (P(n0​))

Words: 42
Mathematical induction OurBigBook.com
The starting instance of a mathematical induction proof, established directly before the inductive step is applied. The implication P(n)⇒P(n+1) alone can be true when every instance is false. For example, ∑j=1n​j=n(n+1)/2+C with C=0 has a formally correct successor calculation but a false base case.

Induction hypothesis

Words: 26
Mathematical induction OurBigBook.com
The assertion assumed for earlier cases during an induction proof. It is a conditional assumption inside the induction step, not an assumption that all cases already hold.

Strong induction (P(n0​),[∀k∈{n0​,…,n}, P(k)]⇒P(n+1))

Words: 764 Articles: 3
Mathematical induction OurBigBook.com
Strong induction establishes a proposition P(n) for all integers n≥n0​. Prove P(n0​); then, for each n≥n0​, assume every P(k) with n0​≤k≤n and prove P(n+1). The induction hypothesis includes all earlier cases, so the inductive step can use whichever smaller indices it needs. It cannot use P(n+1) itself.[ref]
This is useful when a construction breaks into smaller pieces of varying sizes. A prime factorization splits a composite number into smaller integer divisors, which need not be one less than the original integer. A recursive procedure can likewise call itself on several smaller inputs. The available cases should match those dependencies. Strong induction lets the mathematical proof follow the construction rather than forcing every step through the immediately preceding size.
Strong induction with four starting cases
Words: 318
Strong induction OurBigBook.com
Consider a chosen packing problem: batches contain either four or seven identical items, with any nonnegative number of batches allowed. Which integer totals can be formed? The claim is that every total of at least eighteen is attainable:
∀n≥18,∃a,b∈N:n=4a+7b.
(42)
Here a,b count batches, so they must be nonnegative integers; the convention N={0,1,2,…} permits omitting either size. Four direct starting cases are
18=4+7+7,19=4+4+4+7,20=4+4+4+4+4,21=7+7+7.
(43)
If n≥21 and every total from 18 through n is attainable, then n−3≥18 is one of the cases available in the induction hypothesis. Add a batch of four to its representation to obtain n+1. Thus the inductive step applies to every new total from 22 onward. Formally, one can start the strong induction at 18 and handle the next three totals directly before using the uniform step. The finite checks and the propagation together establish all totals, not merely those drawn below.
Checking only 18 and repeatedly adding four would reach only totals congruent to 18 in modular arithmetic modulo four. The four induction base cases supply all four residue classes. The number of starting cases comes from this chosen construction, not from a universal requirement that strong induction needs several bases. A different construction can need different starting information.
The threshold is sharp for these batch sizes. If 17=4a+7b, reducing modulo four gives 3b≡1(mod4), so b≡3(mod4). A nonnegative b would therefore be at least three, giving 7b≥21>17, a contradiction. A finite failed search alone would need an explicit bound on a,b; this short modular arithmetic argument supplies a general obstruction.
Strong induction for factorization existence
Words: 256
Strong induction OurBigBook.com
Every integer n≥2 has a prime factorization. The induction base case 2 is prime. For a larger integer, either it is prime or it is ab, with 2≤a,b<n. The induction hypothesis supplies prime factorizations of both smaller integer divisors; multiplying them gives one for n. This proves existence, while uniqueness requires the additional argument under the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.[ref]
For the chosen number 84, one possible recursive decomposition is
84=6⋅14=(2⋅3)(2⋅7)=22⋅3⋅7.
(44)
The step at 84 needs results for 6 and 14, rather than a result for 83. Each composite number in this factorization tree splits into strictly smaller positive integers, so recursive descent terminates at prime numbers. The tree describes one construction; another choice of integer divisors can give a differently shaped factorization tree.
The same pattern explains the usefulness of strong induction for algorithm correctness. When a recursive procedure returns answers for smaller inputs, the induction hypothesis can justify those answers; the remaining task is to justify how the current call combines them. Strictly decreasing a nonnegative integer size measure establishes termination. Correctness also requires each call's conditions and its combination rule; termination alone does not make an algorithm correct.
Strong induction and accumulated hypotheses
Words: 76
Strong induction OurBigBook.com
Strong induction does not prove more than ordinary mathematical induction. Put Q(n)=⋀k=n0​n​P(k). Ordinary mathematical induction on Q retains the earlier cases and obtains the next one, establishing the same conclusion. Conversely, an ordinary inductive step can ignore the extra cases allowed in a strong induction hypothesis.[ref]
The well-ordering principle gives another view. A least counterexample would have all smaller cases true, so the strong induction step would establish that allegedly false case. The starting case excludes the beginning.

Backward induction proves or computes a finite sequence of statements by starting at its terminal index and stepping toward the initial index.

A counterexample is one instance satisfying a claim’s hypotheses but not its conclusion, and therefore disproves the universal claim.

Structural induction

Words: 181 Articles: 2
Mathematical proof OurBigBook.com
Structural induction proves a property of every recursively generated object by checking the initial objects and showing that every construction rule preserves the property.

Structural induction on lazy lists

Words: 73
Structural induction OurBigBook.com
For an admissible predicate on lazy lists P, prove P(⊥) and P([]), and prove P(xs)⇒P(x:xs) for every possibly partial head x. Constructor induction then establishes P on every finite partial approximation, and admissibility extends it to limits, including infinite lists. Without the bottom value case and the limit condition, ordinary finite structural induction does not justify a claim about infinite data.[ref]

Admissible predicate on lazy lists

Words: 84
Structural induction OurBigBook.com
A predicate on possibly partial lists is admissible when it holds at the limit of every increasing chain of finite approximations on which it holds. Increasing here means replacing a bottom value by more defined information while retaining already defined constructors and values. This closure condition permits a property established for finite approximations to pass to an infinite list. The predicate “the list is finite” lacks this closure: every finite prefix ending in an undefined tail is finite in extent, but their limit may have infinitely many constructors.

Words: 18
Mathematical proof OurBigBook.com
A probability-preserving bijection pairs outcomes of two events without changing their masses, proving the events have equal probability.
